Abstract
Intelligent transportation systems (ITSs), Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication and autonomous driving technologies have brought about significant changes in the modern vehicular network. At the same time, the cyber-attack surface has grown, leading to new and existing advanced security threats for Vehicular Ad hoc Networks (VANETs) and the Internet of Vehicles (IoV). Traditional IDSs that employ static rule-based techniques are often insufficient in the context of the vehicular environment, characterized by dynamic, highly mobile systems with stringent low-latency requirements. Next generation IDS development has shifted to artificial intelligence (AI), which offers adaptive, scalable and data-driven detection capabilities. In this survey, the authors present a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art of AI-driven vehicle IDS in terms of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), federated learning (FL), reinforcement learning (RL), transformer-based techniques, and graph neural network (GNN) designs. We present a multidimensional taxonomy of vehicular attacks, an analysis of existing datasets and their weaknesses, an evaluation of the performance of AI techniques and a study of potential deployment architectures such as edge, fog and cloud. Furthermore, some of the most important open problems are identified, including data scarcity, adversarial robustness, real-time constraints, data utility-privacy conflicts, and standardization gaps. 11. Conclusions
This survey is built to review and analyse the key aspects of artificial intelligence-based intrusion detection systems (AI-IDSs) for vehicular networks across various architectures, communication technologies, advanced techniques, datasets, and attack taxonomies for performance evaluation. It brings together several diverse research areas and thus offers a unified perspective on the newly established cybersecurity of the vehicular division. Several trends emerge from the results: vehicular networks are very complex and hostile cyber-physical systems; nodes exhibit very high mobility; communications are decentralized architectures have stringent latency requirements; and the system has limited resources. In such scenarios, conventional IDSs based on known-signature and rule-based approaches are inherently inappropriate, as they lack the capability to detect zero-day and adaptive attacks.
